title: Data Sources
text:
Each country profile draws on the sources below. Because profiles are submitted by individual country teams, not every profile cites every source — check a profile’s own References section (section 11) for what was actually used there.

DHS StatCompiler / DHS surveys — household survey indicators such as prevalence, mortality, and intervention coverage.
MICS — Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys, used alongside DHS for survey-derived indicators where available.
DHIS2 — routine health information system data behind the incidence and health-system indicators.
Malaria Atlas Project (MAP) — modeled surfaces and administrative boundary layers used in stratification and admin-boundary maps.
Natural Earth — the boundary data behind this site’s own Africa map on the homepage.

Questions about a specific number or map in a profile belong with that country’s own team — see the profile’s References section for citations and contacts.

title: Benin Malaria Epidemiology Summary
text: Benin is a narrow, elongated country in West Africa bordered by Togo, Burkina Faso, Niger, and Nigeria, with a population of roughly 14.5 million (WHO, 2023; World Bank, 2024). Malaria is endemic nationally and remains the leading cause of under-five mortality and a significant cause of adult morbidity, placing Benin among the 15 highest-burden countries globally (WHO World Malaria Report, 2024). This profile consolidates the country’s administrative and demographic context, malaria epidemiology, control history, and health system to support evidence-based planning and correct interpretation of MAP’s model outputs.

title: Benin Malaria Epidemiology Summary
text:
3. Administrative Boundaries
Benin comprises 12 departments, subdivided into 77 communes, further divided into 546 arrondissements, composed of 5,295 villages. The health system, however, is organized around 34 health zones, which do not correspond one-to-one with communes or departments (PMI, 2023), a distinction worth flagging for any stratification or spatial analysis intended to align with programmatic decision-making, since correspondence between department/commune boundaries and health-zone boundaries will need to be resolved before model outputs from this profile can be used at the health-zone level.
Figure: Benin_StudyArea_Map Caption: Administrative departments of Benin, showing the 12 departments and their capitals as well as the number of communes per department, the capital (Porto-Novo, blue), and main city (Cotonou, red)

Source: Institut géographique National du Bénin (IGN-Benin) via Humanitarian Data Exchange, 2026










Figure 1: Administrative geography of Benin: 12 departments and 34 communes.





Source: Administrative boundaries: Malaria Atlas Project (release 202403), retrieved 2026-10-21.

title: Benin Malaria Epidemiology Summary
text:
4. Malaria Situation
Three transmission zones are recognized nationally: a heterogeneous southern coastal zone, a holoendemic central plateau, and a markedly seasonal northern Sahelian zone, with Plasmodium falciparum responsible for 98-100% of infections (PMI, 2023; WHO, 2024). Benin is among the 15 highest-burden countries globally, accounting for an estimated 2% of global malaria cases and 1.7% of global malaria deaths in 2023 (Severe Malaria Observatory, 2024). Malaria remains the leading cause of under-five mortality and accounts for roughly 37–40% of outpatient consultations and 25% of hospital admissions nationally (PMI, 2018). Routine surveillance shows a rising absolute caseload alongside a declining test positivity rate over 2018-2022, consistent with expanding diagnostic access rather than worsening transmission.

title: Benin Malaria Epidemiology Summary
text:
5. History of Malaria (last 20 years)
Benin’s malaria response built out steadily from the mid-2000s: ACTs became first-line treatment in 2004, free LLINs and IPTp were adopted in 2008, and a nationwide mass LLIN campaign followed in 2011 alongside free case management for children under five and pregnant women. IRS was rolled out in phases - Ouémé (2008), expanding south (2010) and north to Atacora (2011) - while the National Malaria Strategic Plan 2017-2021 set the long-term goal of malaria being “no longer a public health problem” by 2030. Seasonal malaria chemoprevention was introduced in 2019 and expanded through 2021, reflecting growing recognition of the seasonal transmission pattern in the north. National parasite prevalence (RDT, children 6-59 months) moved from 25% (2011-12) to 37% (2015), 36% (2017-18), and 32% (2022). The RTS,S malaria vaccine was rolled out in 2024, the most recent addition to the prevention package (Alohoutade et al., 2026).
Figure: Benin_history_timeline Caption: History of malaria control in Benin, 2004–2024, with national parasite prevalence (RDT, children 6–59 months)

Source: Compiled from PMI Benin Malaria Profile; DHS/MIS survey rounds (see References)

title: Benin Malaria Epidemiology Summary
text:
7. Health System
Benin’s health system follows a three-tier pyramidal structure: central (Ministry of Health, national hospitals), intermediate (12 departments, via Departmental Health Directorates), and peripheral (34 health zones, via Health Zone Management Teams). Each reports through DHIS2, with paper forms still used peripherally (PMI, 2023). Community health workers (relais communautaires for prevention/referral, agents de santé communautaires qualifiés for testing/treatment) support the peripheral tier, though only 36 of roughly 1,474 CHWs nationally currently provide malaria testing services. Facility coverage rose from 89% (2005) to 96% (2021), financing runs through a common-basket system with free case management for the highest-risk groups, and DHIS2 reporting completeness reached 99.5% by 2022.
Figure: benin_health_pyramid Caption: Benin health system reporting structure.

Source: U.S. President’s Malaria Initiative (2023). Benin Malaria Profile, PMI FY2024 (see references)

title: Benin Malaria Epidemiology Summary
text:
8. Stratification Maps / SNT
Benin’s stratification has evolved from the coarse MARA/ARMA national risk map, through the NMSP 2017-2021’s three-zone ecological classification, to the 2021 PNLP/Swiss TPH health-zone-level modelling exercise that directly informed Benin’s 2021–2023 Global Fund funding request. The most recent publicly available products are the MARA/ARMA-updated transmission-season map and the MIS 2022 department-level RDT prevalence maps for pregnant women and children under five. Benin is not among the original 10 WHO HBHI countries that underwent the standardized SNT process, so these remain the most current stratification outputs identified for this profile.
Figure: benin_stratification1 Caption: Start month of the malaria transmission season by department

Source: MARA/ARMA, updated with 2021 case data

Figure: benin_stratification2 Caption: Malaria prevalence (RDT) by department, MIS 2022: (1) pregnant women, (2) children under 5

Source: U.S. President’s Malaria Initiative

title: Benin Malaria Epidemiology Summary
text:
9. Environment and Seasonality
Malaria transmission tracks Benin’s north-south climatic gradient: a sub-equatorial, bimodal-rainfall south (transmission starting April), a transitional central plateau (June), and a semi-arid Sahelian north with a single rainy season (July) (MARA/ARMA, 2021). Nationally, peak transmission spans April–October, but this masks the zonal heterogeneity that determines, for example, SMC eligibility in the north, which requires at least 60% of annual cases to fall within a 4-month window (Merle et al., 2023). The Harmattan dry-season wind further suppresses vector breeding and marks the national low-transmission window.

title: Benin Malaria Epidemiology Summary
text:
10. Vector Profile
Plasmodium falciparum causes 98-100% of infections in Benin, transmitted primarily by the Anopheles gambiae complex: An. coluzzii (~91%), An. gambiae s.s. (~8%), and hybrids (~1%), with An. funestus as a secondary vector and An. arabiensis/An. nili also present (PMI, 2023; WHO, 2024). Insecticide resistance is now the central operational constraint: pyrethroid resistance is confirmed at 100% of sites tested, partially restored by PBO synergist, while carbamate resistance is present at 57% of sites, and organophosphate, pirimiphos-methyl, and chlorfenapyr susceptibility remain intact. IRS was phased in from 2008 to 2011 but PMI funding ended in 2021, and the Centre de Recherche Entomologique de Cotonou (CREC) remains the primary source for more granular vector data.
Figure (maps recommended): benin_vector_dry_vs_rainy Caption: Dominant malaria vector species by department in Benin: (1) dry season, (2) rainy season. An. coluzzii predominates nationally in the dry season and in the south year-round; An. gambiae becomes more represented in parts of the north and center during the rainy season, with the exception of Malanville (Alibori), which remains couzzii-dominant in both seasons.

Source: Akpodji S, Agbangla C, Akogbéto M, et al. (2025). Tropical Medicine and Health, 53:147

title: About this platform
text:
Malaria Country Profiles is built by the MAP Data Engineering Team (DET) to give malaria modelers a fast, standardized starting point before they build a model for a given country.
Every profile — regardless of which country team wrote it — follows the same source-backed template: 11 sections covering administrative boundaries, the malaria situation, history, indicator summaries, the health system, stratification/SNT, environment, vector profile, and references. That consistency is the point: you can move from one country’s profile to another and know exactly where to find what you need.

title: About this platform
text:
How profiles are built
Country teams complete a shared submission template — a filled-in content file plus an epi table and supporting exports — and hand it to DET, who format it into the page you’re reading.
See Data Sources for what feeds the template itself, or Help if you’re submitting a profile and have a question.

title: Mozambique Malaria Epidemiology Summary
text: Mozambique sits in southeastern Africa within the WHO African Region, among the five highest-burden malaria countries globally, with roughly 34.6 million people at risk (WHO, 2024). What sets Mozambique apart is that malaria control here is not a targeted, geographically bounded effort: the entire population is classified as at high risk, with no low-risk or malaria-free zones anywhere in the country. This universal exposure, combined with perennial transmission and a north-east to south-west burden gradient, makes malaria control central to the country’s health system, with malaria cases equivalent to about a quarter of all outpatient consultations in 2022 (SIS-MA, via PMI, 2024).

title: Mozambique Malaria Epidemiology Summary
text:
3. Administrative Boundaries
Mozambique lies between latitudes 10°S to 27°S and longitudes 30°E to 41°E, occupying 799,380 km² along the south-east African coast. It is divided into eleven provinces, 154 statutory districts, 457 postos administrativos and 1,712 localidades, alongside a separate elected structure of 65 municipalities (OCHA, 2025). OCHA’s Common Operational Dataset renders 161 admin-2 units because it treats Maputo City’s seven distritos municipais as districts; use 161 for any geospatial work, since the DHIS2 organisation units, the facility registry and the SNT layers are all built on it. Health districts follow the administrative districts, which is what makes district-level stratification operationally tractable. The maps on this page use the Malaria Atlas Project boundary set, which also has 161 district-level units.








Figure 1: Administrative geography of Mozambique: 11 provinces and 161 districts.





Source: Administrative boundaries: Malaria Atlas Project (release 202403), retrieved 2026-10-15.

title: Mozambique Malaria Epidemiology Summary
text:
4. Malaria Situation
Mozambique contributes to more than 3.6% of estimated global malaria cases annually, one of five countries (alongside Nigeria, DRC, Ethiopia, and Uganda) that together account for over half of all global cases, and one of 11 high-burden African countries that account for roughly two-thirds of global cases and deaths (WHO, 2025). WHO estimates about 10.2 million malaria cases and 17,946 deaths in Mozambique in 2024 (WHO, 2025). The national programme’s routine reports for the same year are higher for cases, about 11.5 million, and far lower for deaths, 358 in-hospital deaths, because routine data count only the cases and deaths seen at health facilities (WHO, 2025). Efforts to reduce transmission have resulted in some improvements: cases fell 12% and deaths 1% between 2023 and 2024, but cyclones and extremist-group activity remain the greatest threats to this progress, as the resulting displacement, deaths, and breaks in service provision often leave societies vulnerable (WHO, 2024; WHO, 2025).

title: Mozambique Malaria Epidemiology Summary
text:
5. History of Malaria
Mozambique’s modern programme dates to the re-establishment of the NMCP in 1982, but the decisive shift came in the mid-2000s, when failing monotherapies gave way to artemisinin-based combination therapy and intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy began nationally (MISAU, 2006). Over the following decade the programme built out universal coverage: vector control and parasitological diagnosis, mass insecticide-treated net campaigns, indoor residual spraying in selected high-burden districts and rapid diagnostic tests extended to community level under successive strategic plans in 2012, 2017 and 2023, with nationwide DHIS2 reporting from 2015 giving district-level routine data for the first time; since 2020 the emphasis has moved from uniform national coverage to subnational tailoring, with intervention packages assigned by stratum (MISAU, 2023). The current mix combines pyrethroid chlorfenapyr nets deployed against widespread pyrethroid resistance, targeted IRS, IPTp, seasonal malaria chemoprevention in Nampula (introduced in 2022; the 2024–25 campaign was cancelled in January 2025 amid post-election unrest), universal testing with RDTs followed by artemether-lumefantrine and the R21 vaccine introduced in Zambézia in 2024 though cyclones, COVID-19 and post election unrest have repeatedly interrupted delivery and the 2023-2030 plan remains costed well beyond secured financing (Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, 2024; Malaria Consortium, 2025; GiveWell, 2025; MISAU, 2023; OCHA, 2026).

title: Mozambique Malaria Epidemiology Summary
text:
7. Health System
Public health services reach an estimated 60% of the population, while the private sector is largely limited to major cities (PMI, 2024). There has been progressive investment in health infrastructure, particularly rural healthcare. The health sector is coordinated nationally by the Ministry of Health (MISAU), with implementation devolved to Provincial Health Directorates (DPS) and District Health Services (SDSMAS). There are efforts to decentralise resources and decision-making authority from central to provincial level. The healthcare system is hierarchically structured into four levels:

Levels I and II: primary care, peripheral facilities (health posts and rural clinics).
Levels III and IV: secondary and tertiary care with specialised services.









Figure 3: Organisation of health administration and service delivery, Mozambique.





Source: Country researcher’s compilation (2024 draft). Where the country tab was blank, facility types and roles in malaria control are standard descriptions based on WHO guidance.

Community Health Workers (CHWs)
CHWs, locally known as Agentes Polivalentes Elementares (APEs) play a critical role in healthcare delivery, especially in remote areas. There are 17,648 deployed out of 18,000 planned and 5,595 of these are involved in diagnosing and treating uncomplicated malaria as well as promoting preventive measures, and referring severe cases (End Malaria Global Community Health Dashboard). APEs are keystone for malaria control in rural and remote areas.
Mozambique transitioned from paper based reporting that was aggregated at district, provincial and national level to a DHIS2 based system in 2015. While the initial approach was reliable and consistent, the quality of data did not meet malaria control management needs. Currently a full information M&E system based on the DHIS2 platform collects malaria data. This includes outpatient attendance, testing, and confirmed cases, with disaggregation by age and gender. Facilities with electronic systems fill data directly to the system and paper based records are entered into the system by district health teams. Efforts are underway to strengthen real-time data availability for decision-making.
Routine indicators in DHIS2 include outpatient visits for suspected malaria and laboratory-confirmed cases by rapid diagnostic test (RDT), with age-disaggregated data on positive cases. Periodic household surveys such as IMASIDA (the 2015 Immunization, Malaria and HIV Indicators Survey) add population-based data on treatment-seeking behaviour, bed-net coverage and use, and coverage of interventions.


Geographic location of health facilities
Of the facilities mapped, 63 are hospitals (secondary or tertiary level). The largest numbers are in Nampula (10) and Cabo Delgado (7); every province has at least one hospital recorded in this dataset.








Figure 4: Geographic location of 1,580 health facilities in Mozambique (7 tertiary, 56 secondary, 1,517 primary).





Source: Mozambique health facilities, Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX). Province from facility coordinates and MAP boundaries. Administrative boundaries: Malaria Atlas Project (release 202403), retrieved 2026-10-15.
The 1,580 geolocated facilities are unevenly distributed across the 11 provinces, with Sofala (231), Zambezia (229) and Nampula (210) together holding 42% of the national total, while Cidade de Maputo accounts for just 39. Density tells a different story from counts: Cidade de Maputo has 1,140 facilities per 10,000 km² against 12.8 in Tete.








Figure 5: Number of health facilities by province and level of care, Mozambique (total 1,580).





Source: Mozambique health facilities, Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX). Province from facility coordinates and MAP boundaries. Administrative boundaries: Malaria Atlas Project (release 202403), retrieved 2026-10-15.

title: Mozambique Malaria Epidemiology Summary
text:
8. Stratification Maps / SNT
Mozambique uses maps to inform decision making and planning. A structured approach to optimizing malaria interventions in Mozambique involves using complementary analytical methods. It begins with spatial analysis of malaria burden to prioritize high-impact areas. Empirical data analysis and mathematical models help refine intervention targeting by evaluating past interventions and predicting optimal strategies. Cost-effectiveness analysis ensures interventions maximize case reductions within a fixed budget over five years. Finally, operational feasibility adjustments account for logistical and geographic constraints, ensuring interventions are practical and effectively implemented. This multi-faceted approach enhances the impact and efficiency of malaria control efforts. In addition to prevalence and incidence maps, risk maps and vulnerability to epidemics are mapped at district level. This aids with tailoring of interventions.






Figure 6: Malaria incidence trend at district level




Source: National Malaria Strategic Plan (NMSP) of Mozambique: 2023 – 2030 https://mesamalaria.org/resource-hub/national-malaria-strategic-plan-nmsp-of-mozambique-2023-2030/







Figure 7: Malaria deaths trend at district level (legend: deaths per 100,000 population; “Óbitos por malária por 100 000 habitantes”)




Source: National Malaria Strategic Plan (NMSP) of Mozambique: 2023 – 2030 https://mesamalaria.org/resource-hub/national-malaria-strategic-plan-nmsp-of-mozambique-2023-2030/







Figure 8: Tailored Intervention Packages based on burden. Legend translation: Pacote Principal = core package; Pacote Principal Adicional = core package plus; Pacote Ideal = ideal package; RTIs Nova Geração = new-generation insecticide-treated nets; PMC = perennial malaria chemoprevention; SMC = seasonal malaria chemoprevention; PIDOM = indoor residual spraying (focalizada = targeted); Vigilância baseada no caso = case-based surveillance; Vacina = vaccine




Source: National Malaria Strategic Plan (NMSP) of Mozambique: 2023 – 2030 https://mesamalaria.org/resource-hub/national-malaria-strategic-plan-nmsp-of-mozambique-2023-2030/

Parasite prevalence by RDT in children aged 6–59 months follows a steep north–south gradient, exceeding 33% across the northern and central provinces and peaking at 54.7% in Nampula, falling to 10–20% in Tete, Inhambane and Manica, and approaching zero in the far south (5.7% in Gaza, 0.3% in Maputo Province and 0.0% in Cidade de Maputo; 2022–23 DHS, IDS).

title: Mozambique Malaria Epidemiology Summary
text:
9. Environment and Seasonality
Transmission is sustained year-round by warm temperatures: mean monthly temperature stays above 18 ℃ in every province except the Manica highlands, so the thermal threshold for sporogonic development of Plasmodium falciparum is rarely a constraint, while low-lying coastal and riverine terrain and abundant surface water provide continuous Anopheles breeding habitat (MISAU, 2023; NASA Langley Research Center, 2025). Intensity follows a north-south ecological gradient, from the wet, densely populated northern provinces to the drier south, with mean annual rainfall falling from 1,403 mm in Nampula to 605 mm in Gaza and mean annual temperature ranging from 25.4 ℃ in Zambezia down to 21.2 ℃ on the Manica plateau, the one area cool enough in June-August (16.3 ℃ in July) to slow the parasite’s development materially (NASA Langley Research Center, 2025). Because temperature is permissive almost everywhere, rainfall sets the timing: a single wet season from December to April concentrates precipitation (362 mm in January in the north against 128 mm in the south) and, with cases lagging rainfall by roughly six to ten weeks (Harp et al., 2021), transmission peaks from December to April (PMI, 2024), earlier and sharper in the north and centre than in the south, where transmission is lower and more seasonal (MISAU, 2023).






Figure 9: Mean Monthly Rainfall (mm), 1991-2020




Source: NASA POWER, parameter PRECTOTCORR (precipitation corrected, MERRA-2), 30-year climatology January 1991 – December 2020, retrieved at each province’s representative interior point via the POWER Climatology API. https://power.larc.nasa.gov/







Figure 10: Rainfall zones and mean annual rainfall by province, Mozambique




Source: NASA POWER, parameter PRECTOTCORR (precipitation corrected, MERRA-2), 30-year climatology January 1991 – December 2020, retrieved at each province’s representative interior point via the POWER Climatology API. https://power.larc.nasa.gov/

title: Mozambique Malaria Epidemiology Summary
text:
10. Vector Profile
Malaria transmission in Mozambique is sustained by three primary vectors Anopheles funestus, An. arabiensis and An. gambiae sensu stricto with the saltwater breeding An. merus contributing along the southern and central coast; species-distribution models place An. funestus and An. arabiensis across virtually the whole country, while An. gambiae s.s. is concentrated in the wetter north and centre and An. merus is restricted to the coastal strip (Sinka et al., 2010; Wiebe et al., 2017). Recent entomological work documents multiple insecticide resistance in An. funestus (Kiuru et al., 2025); the monitoring record is summarised in Table 5 and described below. P450-mediated pyrethroid resistance, shown by the restoration of deltamethrin mortality with piperonyl butoxide (PBO), is the operational rationale for the shift to dual-active-ingredient and PBO nets and for rotating IRS products away from pyrethroids.








Figure 11: Modelled relative probability of occurrence of 4 dominant malaria vector species by district, Mozambique. The surfaces are long-term modelled distributions published in 2010 and 2017, not estimates for a single year. Grey areas have no data in the surface.





Source: Malaria Atlas Project (malariaAtlas package, retrieved 2026-10-16): Anopheles funestus; Anopheles arabiensis Patton, 1905; Anopheles gambiae Giles, 1902; Anopheles merus Dönitz, 1902. Publication year by species: An. funestus (2017), An. arabiensis (2010), An. gambiae s.s. (2017), An. merus (2017). Each district shows the mean of the surface within it. Administrative boundaries: Malaria Atlas Project (release 202403), retrieved 2026-10-15.

Vector and parasite species
Malaria in Mozambique is primarily caused by Plasmodium falciparum, the most virulent malaria parasite. The vector species are described above, and Table 4 summarises the parasite and vector facts.

Insecticide resistance in Mozambique has followed a clear trajectory over twenty-five years of monitoring. In collections from 2000–02, Anopheles funestus s.s. was already pyrethroid-resistant in the far south but fully susceptible to DDT and to the organophosphate malathion everywhere tested (Casimiro et al., 2006). By 2006–10 the same pyrethroid resistance had reached central Mozambique, appearing in An. funestus in Mocuba, Zambézia, while DDT and deltamethrin still killed 100% of mosquitoes (Abílio et al., 2011). In collections from 2021–22 in Mopeia, also Zambézia, An. funestus s.l. was resistant to all four classes tested: 14% mortality to deltamethrin, 37% to bendiocarb, 67% to pirimiphos-methyl and 79% to DDT with piperonyl butoxide restoring deltamethrin mortality from 8% (deltamethrin alone in the synergist assay, a separate batch of wild-caught females) to 80% (Kiuru et al., 2025). Two features of that last result matter operationally: the organophosphate reading, because pirimiphos-methyl is a mainstay IRS product, and the PBO restoration, because it identifies cytochrome P450 monooxygenases as the mechanism and is the direct evidence base for PBO and dual-active-ingredient nets.
